prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of the gains from trade and of firm-level trade data

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. I now prefer B026 (Melitz and Helpman) as a single part, and B009 becomes my first alternative. The change rests on the substance of the exchange, not on support counts. Melitz (2003) is the originating model of firm heterogeneity and selection. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) on exporting versus FDI, together with Helpman's wider heterogeneous-firm agenda, gives a defensible second name. The advance moved the unit of analysis from the industry to the firm and made reallocation across firms and exporter selection channels for gains from trade. More than twenty years of firm-level administrative and customs data from many countries have tested its central claim. As an economic historian I weigh this link between a framework and newly assembled micro data heavily, because it is what lets a claim be checked. Hjalmarsson and Fredriksson answered my round-1 worry about the 2008 prize persuasively. Representative-firm new trade theory explained intra-industry trade and location, whereas selection and reallocation is a different mechanism, tested on data that did not exist for the earlier theory. Hassler's reply to Fredriksson also accepts that the Eaton-Kortum quantitative line answers a different question. That weakens my second reservation. B009 has the more coherent three-name credit, but I have to weigh the 2024 institutions prize and the weaker identification of cross-country constitutional estimates more heavily than I did in round 1. Several colleagues raised both points and my answers did not fully dispose of them. I also note that B009 sits close to my own field, which is a reason to be stricter with it, not more lenient.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary is the main reservation. Bernard and Jensen established the exporter-premium facts that the theory later explained. Eaton and Kortum, and Redding, built a parallel quantitative line. None of them is on this ballot entry, and a Melitz-Helpman prize could be read as under-crediting the empirical establishment of the field. Helpman's claim is also spread across other trade work, so the Committee would have to say why he and not a Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum contributor is the second name. The proximity to the 2008 trade prize is reduced but not removed. The size of the welfare gains depends on functional-form assumptions such as the productivity distribution. Finally, B026's breadth of influence is narrower than that of the New Keynesian framework in B012, whose attribution I still cannot resolve. I have not independently verified citation counts or priority claims.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first and reads firm heterogeneity as distinct from the 2008 prize. She argues that a conceptual advance, validated on firm-level data across countries, has held up under replication. She also ranks B009 second but puts B026 ahead because of the 2024 adjacency and weaker identification of the Persson-Tabellini results.
responses.response: I now accept this ordering, and it is the main reason I moved. My round-1 reply defended B009's distinctness from the 2024 prize, but I could not show that the cross-country constitutional estimates meet the same evidentiary standard as the firm-level trade evidence. I agree with her that the citation should be written around the theoretical framework of heterogeneity and selection, and should not claim to honour all firm-level trade research. I also agree that omitting Redding is an attribution call that the Committee should state explicitly.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from B039 to B026. He treats Melitz as the originating model and Helpman as the natural second laureate. He says Bernard and Jensen's exporter facts and Eaton-Kortum's quantitative line are real omissions, but he argues that the heterogeneous-firm framework is already well identified and tested, so the omissions do not justify waiting.
responses.response: His argument that the omissions are not serious enough to delay is the one that moved me most on attribution. A prize is for the framework that reorganised the field, and the empirical pioneers' contribution is recognised in the citation's emphasis on firm-level data without being credited by name. I still think the Committee must acknowledge that choice openly. On B039, which he mentions in relation to my third-place ranking, I agree that task and skill-bias work and the trade-shock work may be two discoveries, so I do not rely on it here.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B007 and ranks B026 second. He asks whether the second name should be Helpman or a contributor from the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line, and says this attribution question is why he still prefers the two-author Kiyotaki-Moore credit.
responses.response: I take the attribution question as legitimate and the Committee should answer it on the record. My answer is that the theoretical framework is Melitz's, and Helpman's joint work with Melitz and Yeaple is part of the same line, so the pair credits one conceptual advance. Bernard-Jensen is an empirical-facts contribution and Eaton-Kortum is a Ricardian quantitative line, which answer different questions. I accept that this is a judgement call and that it cannot be settled by the ballot entry alone. I rank B007 as my second alternative because I agree its credit is cleaner, but I weigh its overlap with the 2022 prize and its thinner empirical identification more heavily than he does.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, ranks B012 first but lists B026 as an alternative. He accepts that selection and the extensive margin were not covered by the 2008 prize, but says B026 is not as clean as the two-name proposal suggests because Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are uncredited and Helpman also appears under the trade-politics entry.
responses.response: I agree that B026 is not free of attribution problems, and I do not claim it is. I weigh them differently from B012's. In B012 the problem is which three of eight names carry credit for what is arguably several separable discoveries. In B026 it is whether the central discovery is already well identified, and I think it is. On Helpman appearing under another entry, a laureate's other work does not weaken his claim here, and the citation should be tied to heterogeneous-firm selection and not to his wider agenda. I do not discount B012's policy reach. I still cannot see how the Committee would choose its trio without leaving out contributors it would regard as essential.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee finds Helpman a defensible second name, or prefers a Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum contributor or Redding for the empirical and quantitative strands.
Whether the firm-heterogeneity advance is distinct enough from the 2008 trade prize. I think it is, but I cannot settle it from the written record alone.
How much weight to give the functional-form sensitivity of the welfare gains, relative to the robustness of the qualitative selection and reallocation result.
Whether B009 should rank above B026 if the Committee judges the 2024 overlap and the identification concerns to be smaller than I now do, and whether Besley belongs in the credit.
I have not independently verified citation counts, priority claims or the details of the credited authors' contributions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred part. It lists no co-authorship, institutional tie or collaboration with Melitz or Helpman. My field of economic history is close to the historical and comparative applications of B009, which is now an alternative, and that is subject proximity and not a personal conflict. My co-authors Cermeño and Lindvall, and my Lund colleagues, are not candidates. Teorell's unresolved question about which Persson co-authored with him bears on B009 only. I disclose these without adjudicating them.
